summary: Over 14 days, glucose control is broadly good but not fully safe to tighten: average glucose was 121.6 mg/dL, TIR 86.0%, CV 32.6%, with recurrent hypoglycemia exposure (5.1% below range, lows to 41-42 mg/dL) and intermittent afternoon hyperglycemia. The data are strong enough to review settings, but the absence of carb logs and the presence of corrections, temp targets, and a mid-period profile switch make causal attribution incomplete.

analysis_steps.findings: CGM and Nightscout telemetry quality are good enough for review. Coverage was 98.7% with 3995 valid glucose entries, 0 invalid entries, 0 duplicates, 10 gaps, and a largest gap of 65 minutes. The last entry was near the period end, so the dataset is current. The profile package is complete and includes basal, CR, ISF, DIA, SMB/UAM, max basal, max IOB, and target segments.

A profile switch occurred during the period, which limits clean attribution across the boundary.

analysis_steps.findings: The main safety constraint is recurrent low glucose exposure alongside some afternoon highs. Average glucose and TIR are solid, but the below-range exposure and low nadirs mean any insulin-strengthening change should be conservative and sequenced. The best overall pattern is not severe sustained hyperglycemia; it is mixed variability with lows and late-day rises.
evidence: daily highs to 286-293 mg/dL on 2026-08-15 and 2026-08-18

analysis_steps.findings: Local-time glucose is fairly stable overnight and early morning, while the clearest rise is in the afternoon and early evening. However, the afternoon highs overlap with corrections, temp targets, and automation responses, so they cannot be assigned to basal alone. The late-evening period then trends lower, which argues against blindly strengthening late-day basal. The target schedule is already modest and does not obviously explain the pattern.

analysis_steps.findings: The profile is internally coherent, but CR, ISF, and DIA cannot be cleanly judged from this dataset. Correction windows are mixed, and the lack of carb entries prevents any meal-bolus analysis that would normally validate CR. DIA of 10 hours and dynamic sensitivity may be reasonable in this AAPS setup, but the telemetry does not isolate whether that choice is optimal.

analysis_steps.findings: SMB and UAM are enabled and actively functioning. The observed loop statuses and temp basal entries show the system using microboluses and UAM-style responses. This looks like intended behavior, not a misconfiguration. The presence of SMB without COB is not inherently unsafe here because the dataset contains no carb entries and the automation is clearly operating within its design.

analysis_steps.findings: Autosens is disabled, but dynamic sensitivity is enabled, so sensitivity adjustment is not absent. The observed sensitivity_ratio around 1.0 is a neutral current adjustment, not a sign of a disabled system. Max basal and max IOB are far above observed delivery and do not appear to be limiting the system. The main point is that current automation limits do not look like the cause of the late-day highs or lows.

analysis_steps.findings: A meal-bolus strategy cannot be validated because there are no carb entries and no declared meal-strategy fields. The observed therapy windows are mostly correction-based and heavily confounded by SMB/UAM, temp targets, and temporary basal changes. That means any inference about prebolus timing or immediate bolus percentage would be speculative. The safest interpretation is to avoid changing bolus behavior without meal logs.

analysis_steps.findings: There is no direct evidence for e-carbs in the package. Because carb treatment entries are absent, no e-carb amount, offset, or duration can be assessed. The telemetry does not support turning the observed delayed rises into an e-carb recommendation. Any apparent delayed rise could instead be due to CR, bolus timing, IOB, correction stacking, or SMB/UAM behavior.

analysis_steps.findings: The integrated picture supports keeping the current profile and automation settings unchanged for now. Overnight control is acceptable, the afternoon rise is real but not isolated, and the lows make broad insulin strengthening risky. The strongest next step is not a parameter change but better observation with meal logging so the team can separate meal effects from correction and automation effects. No profile row change is supported by the current evidence, so the profile recommendation is keep.

strengths.title: High-quality CGM coverage
strengths.description: The record is strong enough for review, with 98.7% coverage, no invalid entries, and no duplicates.

strengths.title: Good average glucose and time in range
strengths.description: Average glucose and TIR are solid overall despite variability, suggesting the system is working reasonably well.

strengths.title: Overnight is broadly stable
strengths.description: The overnight and early-morning windows are relatively controlled compared with the afternoon rise.

strengths.title: Automation ceilings are not being hit
strengths.description: Observed rates and IOB are well below the max basal and max IOB limits, so those ceilings do not look like the current bottleneck.

issues.title: Recurrent hypoglycemia exposure
issues.description: Below-range time is 5.1% and the data include lows down to the low-40s mg/dL, so tighter insulin changes would need caution.

issues.title: Afternoon hyperglycemia window

issues.title: Mid-period profile switch limits clean comparison

recommendations.title: Keep the profile unchanged for now
recommendations.description: The current data do not cleanly separate basal, CR, ISF, or DIA effects from meals and automation. A profile change would be hard to justify safely before better observation is available.

suggested_change.review: Retain all current basal, CR, ISF, target, and DIA settings for now and reassess only after logged meal and fasting-like observations are available.

recommendations.title: Wait for logged meal data before changing bolus strategy
recommendations.description: The dataset does not contain meal carb timing or prebolus information, so prebolus, immediate bolus percentage, and e-carbs should not be altered based on this record alone.

suggested_change.review: Keep the current bolus approach unchanged and collect timestamped meal logs before considering any prebolus or split-bolus adjustment.

profile_recommendation.rationale: The overnight and early-morning pattern is fairly stable, while the afternoon highs and late-day lows are too confounded by corrections, temp targets, SMB/UAM, and the mid-period profile switch to support a safe basal change. Strengthening basal now could worsen the recurrent lows, and there is no fasting-like evidence that a specific segment is clearly wrong.
profile_recommendation.next_check: Review 3 to 5 logged overnight or fasting-like periods, plus one logged afternoon meal window, before revisiting any basal segment.
profile_recommendation.recommendation: Keep the current basal profile unchanged and verify with logged, low-confound observations before considering any basal adjustment.

parameter_decisions.rationale: Overnight glucose is broadly stable and there is no fasting-like window proving this segment is too low or too high. The observed lows are not isolated to this segment and may be driven by corrections or automation. Changing basal together with other settings would be unsafe without cleaner attribution.
Early-morning glucose is acceptable overall and there is no isolated dawn-pattern evidence that this segment needs adjustment. Later rises and lows remain confounded by meal and correction effects.

Morning values do not show a clear basal failure separate from meal and automation effects. Because recurrent lows are present elsewhere, increasing basal here without a cleaner test could worsen safety.
Late-morning patterns do not isolate basal need from meal timing. The available data do not justify changing this segment independently.

Although local-time glucose rises in the afternoon, the rise overlaps with corrections, temp targets, SMB/UAM, and a profile switch, so it cannot be assigned to this segment alone. The later 18:00-19:00 lows also argue against an unverified increase.
The 18:00 local window already shows substantial below-range exposure. Raising this segment would increase low risk without clean evidence that basal is the cause of the evening pattern.
Evening glucose trends lower and below-range time is elevated around this window. A stronger basal here would be difficult to justify and could worsen hypoglycemia.
There are no carb logs or meal-linked responses to validate a change. The mixed correction windows and active SMB/UAM make it impossible to separate CR from other influences.
No meal data are available to test this ratio, and the observed pattern does not isolate early-morning meal handling from corrections or overnight variability.
Morning and mid-day responses are confounded by missing meal logs. The current evidence does not support a safe CR change.

Afternoon hyperglycemia is present, but it is not cleanly attributable to a meal ratio because corrections, automation, and temp targets overlap that period. Changing this CR now would be speculative.
No evening meal data were provided. The late-evening lows make a stronger ratio potentially risky, and there is no direct evidence that this segment is wrong.
Correction responses are mixed and dynamic sensitivity is already active. There is no isolated correction challenge that supports changing ISF safely, especially with recurrent lows.
The overnight target is already modest and overnight control is broadly acceptable. Raising or lowering the target would not be the first safe move given the current low exposure and confounding.
The daytime target is not clearly the cause of the afternoon highs, and the current data do not justify changing it before meal and correction causes are separated.
There is no clean evidence that the late-night target is responsible for the observed lows or highs. A target change would be less safe than better observation.
DIA cannot be validated from the available windows because insulin action is mixed with SMB/UAM, temp basals, and corrections. No data justify changing it now.
The telemetry shows SMB and UAM are functioning as intended and are part of the current control strategy. There is no safety reason to disable them based on this dataset.

This activation logic is internally consistent and matches the observed use of SMB/UAM. The absence of carb entries means COB-gated behavior cannot be tested, but that is not a reason to change the setting.

parameter_decisions.current_value: smb_interval_minutes=3 min; max_smb_basal_minutes=15 min; max_uam_smb_basal_minutes=20 min
parameter_decisions.suggested_value: smb_interval_minutes=3 min; max_smb_basal_minutes=15 min; max_uam_smb_basal_minutes=20 min
parameter_decisions.rationale: The short SMB interval and limits align with the observed microbolusing behavior and do not appear to be causing a safety ceiling problem. The pattern issues are more likely upstream than in these frequency limits.

parameter_decisions.parameter: AAPS / max basal and max IOB limits
parameter_decisions.rationale: Observed delivery never approaches these ceilings. The system is not being held back by max basal or max IOB in the supplied data.
Dynamic sensitivity is active, so sensitivity adjustment is not disabled. Sensitivity_ratio values near 1 are neutral rather than a fault. There is no isolated test that supports changing this group.
The dataset contains no carb entries and no e-carb observations, so there is no evidence to tune absorption settings. Changing this model without meal-linked data would be speculative.

meal_strategy_summary.suggestion: Keep the current meal approach conservative: do not change prebolus timing or immediate bolus percentage yet, continue SMB/UAM as configured, and do not add routine e-carbs until meal-linked logs show a repeatable delayed-rise pattern.
meal_strategy_summary.rationale: The record has no carb entries and no declared meal-strategy fields, so meal handling cannot be validated. The observed highs and lows are strongly confounded by corrections, SMB/UAM, temporary targets, and a profile switch, which makes it unsafe to infer a new bolus or e-carb strategy from this dataset alone.
meal_strategy_summary.next_observation: Log a few repeat meals with carb amount, meal time, and any prebolus timing so 0-6 hour CGM response can be matched to the actual meal rather than to correction or automation effects.

exceptions.pattern: A specific meal repeatedly causes lows within about 2 hours
exceptions.suggestion: Reduce front-loading for that meal type instead of adding e-carbs.
exceptions.rationale: Early lows would increase the risk of stacking insulin on top of an already low baseline and would argue against a stronger prebolus.

exceptions.pattern: A specific meal repeatedly rises late at about 2-4 hours
exceptions.suggestion: First verify the meal with logs before considering any e-carb or bolus-split adjustment.
exceptions.rationale: Late rises could be caused by absorption, CR, timing, IOB, or SMB/UAM, and the current data do not separate those causes.

implementation_steps.action: Keep the current profile unchanged and collect logged meal observations before revisiting basal, CR, ISF, or DIA.
Keep SMB/UAM and dynamic sensitivity unchanged because they appear to be operating within expected safety limits.
Use meal logs to evaluate prebolus timing, immediate bolus behavior, and whether any delayed-rise meals truly justify e-carbs.
Review one setting at a time only after a cleaner observation window is available.

education.note: Without carb logs, it is hard to tell whether a rise or fall comes from the meal, the correction, the basal profile, or SMB/UAM.
Because lows reached the low-40s mg/dL, any change that increases insulin effect should be treated cautiously and tested one step at a time.
A neutral sensitivity_ratio around 1 is not a failure; it just means the dynamic adjustment is currently near baseline.

safety_notes.note: This is decision-support content only. The user must independently verify every proposed change, make changes one at a time, and monitor glucose closely.
Do not change dependent insulin-delivery settings together, because the current data cannot separate their effects safely.
Given the recurrent lows, avoid increasing basal, tightening CR, or strengthening ISF simultaneously.
